While this ruling is great it only specifically covers the direct method for gathering location information. Our local law enforcement doesn't have the money for cell site simulators, so officers ask us to contact cell service providers and have them provide the location information obtained for 911 routing. Most service providers have a standard of there being a "real threat to life" before they will release this information, so when the police ask us to trace phones for property crimes the answer is always "No." But of course even the "threat to life" standard doesn't pass the Fourth Amendment test without probable cause and a warrant, and should result in charges being dismissed if they stem from the information gained.

For anyone who may not be aware, the 911 system is allowed to request your location information under certain circumstances without a warrant. The two scenarios we most often encounter are: if you place a 911 call and are disconnected, and we are unable to get you back on the line; or if there is a "reasonable presumption" that a subscriber would call 911 if they could (think someone locked in the trunk of a car or something). Even these limited circumstances could open themselves up to abuses, so each individual must decide for themselves whether the threat to privacy is worth the potential benefit of our being able to find you if you get lost in the woods, etc.

I'm only one man, but I am extremely protective of the Fourth Amendment while I'm on duty; I've given Constitutional law seminars to homicide detectives who couldn't fathom why we couldn't request a phone trace on a suspect without a warrant. Don't count on having someone like me in your locality, though; I'm very much in the minority in my field.
